message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
Here's everything, starting with tomorrow's route.

## Route: B, then A, then C

This is the **only order that works**:

- **C must be last**, because it won't accept anything before 11:00.
- **B must be first.** The earliest A can be finished is 09:15 (arriving 09:00, unloading 15 minutes). Driving to B then gets you there at 09:40, after the shop opens.

**Timeline:**

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B** (20 min drive) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B ✓ done well before 09:30 opening |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive to A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at **A** ✓ within 09:00–10:00 window |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive to C (40 min) |
| **10:25–10:55** | **30-minute break near C** |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at **C** ✓ not before 11:00 |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive back to depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at depot** |

**Warning: there's no slack at the end.** Unloading at C can't start before 11:00, and C to the depot takes 45 minutes, so the van can't be back before 12:00 exactly in any order. Any delay at C, such as waiting for someone to sign or traffic on the way back, makes the van late. Two options:

- **Call C today** and ask whether they can take the delivery at 10:45, or even 10:30. The break can then move earlier or to the end.
- **Warn whoever needs the van at 12:00** that it may be 10–15 minutes late.

The morning half has some slack: B is finished 25 minutes before the shop opens, and A is within its window. Any early delays can be absorbed there.

## Names for the van

- **Dovetail** (a classic woodworking joint)
- **The Chesterfield**
- **Sideboard Sid**
- **Vanity Unit** (a furniture pun)
- **The Restoration Wagon**
- **French Polish**

## Friendlier driver text

> Hi [Name], your driver [Driver's name] is on the way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. Please make sure someone's home to receive it. Thanks!

## Three checks before handing over furniture

1. **Condition.** Look over the piece in good light for any scratches, chips, dents or marks on the finish that weren't there when it was loaded. Point out anything you find to the customer before they sign.
2. **Completeness and function.** Check that all parts are present (shelves, keys, handles, legs, fittings), and that drawers and doors open and close smoothly.
3. **Right item, in the right place.** Confirm it's the correct piece for that customer. Place it where they want it, then ask them to look it over and confirm they're happy.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed, ideally signed on a phone or tablet at the door, with a photo of the delivered item attached.** It's quicker, can't get lost, and the photo protects you if a damage claim comes in later. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who prefer them, as some older customers do.

## "Proof of delivery," in a line

> **Proof of delivery** is a signed record, often with a photo, showing that the customer received their item in good condition at a particular time.

## Evening-before text

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Business] arrives tomorrow between [time] and [time]. Reply or call [number] if that is a problem. Thanks!

With realistic details filled in, it comes to about **147 characters**, for example:

> Hi Sarah, your furniture from Oakleaf Restoration arrives tomorrow between 9:00 and 10:00. Reply or call 07700 900123 if that is a problem. Thanks!

Two tips to keep it to one message:

- **Long names push it over 160.** If the customer's name plus your business name exceed about 25 characters, shorten the business name (for example, "Oakleaf" instead of "Oakleaf Restoration").
- **Avoid curly apostrophes, emojis and special characters.** A single one switches the whole text to a different encoding with a **70-character** limit, splitting it into several messages. That's why the draft says "that is" rather than "that's." If you use an apostrophe, make sure it's the plain straight kind (').
